definition: Fuzzy logic is a form of many-valued logic in which the truth value of variables may be any real number between 0 and 1.
details: It is employed to handle the concept of partial truth, where the truth value may range between completely true and completely false. By contrast, in Boolean logic, the truth values of variables may only be the integer values 0 or 1. The term fuzzy logic was introduced with the 1965 proposal of fuzzy set theory by mathematician Lotfi Zadeh. Basic fuzzy logic had, however, been studied since the 1920s, as infinite-valued logic—notably by Łukasiewicz and Tarski. The works of Zadeh and Joseph Goguen in the 1960s and 1970s went further by considering issues such as linguistic variables and lattices. Fuzzy logic is based on the observation that people make decisions based on imprecise and non-numerical information. Fuzzy models or fuzzy sets are mathematical means of representing vagueness and imprecise information (hence the term fuzzy). These models have the capability of recognising, representing, manipulating, interpreting, and using data and information that are vague and lack certainty. Fuzzy logic has been applied to many fields, from control theory to artificial intelligence.

explainer.lead: Fuzzy logic lets a statement be partly true, rather than forcing every answer to be simply true or false. It provides a mathematical way to represent vague, imprecise information, making it useful for decision-making, control theory, and artificial intelligence.

tiers.eli5: Think of a dimmer switch instead of a light switch that can only be on or off. Fuzzy logic works similarly: something can be somewhat true, mostly true, or anywhere in between. This helps computers work with descriptions such as “warm” or “fairly high” without pretending they are exact measurements.
tiers.practitioner: Fuzzy models and fuzzy sets are used to represent and manipulate vague information in settings such as control systems and artificial intelligence. Inputs can retain degrees of truth between 0 and 1 instead of being forced into binary categories. A design pitfall is collapsing those degrees back into 0/1 decisions too early, discarding the partial-truth information the approach is intended to preserve.
tiers.paperLevel: Formally, fuzzy logic is many-valued: a variable’s truth value t may be any real number in [0, 1], whereas Boolean logic permits only 0 or 1. The term was introduced with Lotfi Zadeh’s 1965 proposal of fuzzy set theory, although basic fuzzy logic had been studied since the 1920s as infinite-valued logic, notably by Łukasiewicz and Tarski. Zadeh and Joseph Goguen extended the work in the 1960s and 1970s through topics including linguistic variables and lattices.

explainer.example: Suppose a description of “warm” has truth value 0.7 while “hot” has truth value 0.2. A fuzzy model retains both partial assessments, rather than declaring the situation simply warm or not warm, and can use them when forming a decision.

usedIn.name: Control theory
usedIn.detail: Represents imprecise information and partial truth when making control decisions.

usedIn.name: Artificial intelligence
usedIn.detail: Supports the representation, interpretation, and use of data that are vague or uncertain.

explainer.intuition: Human decisions often rely on imprecise, non-numerical descriptions rather than crisp categories. Fuzzy logic captures that flexibility by allowing truth to range continuously between completely false and completely true.
howItWorks: Start with information that is vague or imprecise.
Represent it using fuzzy models or fuzzy sets.
Assign truth values anywhere in the real interval [0, 1].
Manipulate and interpret those values instead of reducing them to 0 or 1.
Use the resulting partial-truth assessments in decisions or control.
explainer.whyItMatters: It gives mathematics and computing a way to recognise and work with vagueness instead of treating every statement as absolutely true or false. That makes it applicable across fields from control theory to artificial intelligence.
misconceptions: It is not merely Boolean logic with extra labels: its truth values can be any real number between 0 and 1.
Its study did not begin in 1965; infinite-valued logic had been studied since the 1920s, before Zadeh introduced the term fuzzy logic.

diagram.caption: Fuzzy logic turns vague information into partial-truth assessments that can inform decisions or control.
